prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks through asset prices and credit, and thereby explaining credit cycles

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore's collateral-constraint model is a single, sharply defined mechanism. Borrowing limits tied to asset values turn small, temporary shocks into large and persistent fluctuations. The mechanism has been absorbed into quantitative macro, banking and macroprudential analysis, and the 2007-09 crisis confirmed its relevance. As a corporate-finance economist I find it persuasive because it is the same logic as financial contracting under limited enforcement: collateral and balance-sheet strength determine who can borrow, and the effects aggregate. The attribution is as clean as any on the shortlist, since the 1997 paper is a two-author contribution with a very large follow-on literature. After nearly thirty years it needs no further confirmation. I have reconsidered my opening ranking in light of colleagues' arguments. I still place this first, but B027 is a close second and I would not object strongly to it.
statement.case_against: The contribution is mainly theoretical, and direct empirical identification of the amplification magnitudes is thinner than for the labour and trade candidates. The 2022 prize (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) covers adjacent ground on financial crises, and a prize here risks looking like macro-finance crowding. A two-person award also leaves out Gertler, whose financial-accelerator and later intermediation work is central, and possibly Gilchrist. B027 has a larger documented policy footprint and broader consensus among colleagues, so my preference could reflect field affinity with finance more than the relative importance of the work.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first. He argues that Kiyotaki and Moore are the clear originators of the collateral-amplification mechanism, that Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the adjacent accelerator strand, and that the 2022 overlap is a real risk.
responses.response: I agree that a two-name award keeps attribution clean and that the originator claim is unambiguous. I am less comfortable dismissing the 2022 overlap than you are. Bernanke's accelerator work is already recognised, but the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is dynamic and works through asset prices, not through bank runs or intermediation. I think that difference is real and that the committee can defend it. Where I qualify your view is on Gertler. His later intermediation work with Kiyotaki is substantial, so the committee should state explicitly why it is not crediting him, not treat the omission as obvious.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B012 first and would credit only Autor and Hanson in B027. He sees the core contributions as separable and notes that the Acemoglu task-framework work complicates credit. He also treats the 2022 prize as a reason to doubt the appetite for another prize in the Kiyotaki-Moore area.
responses.response: Your point that the task framework and the China-shock evidence are separable is fair, and it is why I treat B027's attribution as its weakest feature. I would resist reading the 2022 prize as crowding out B006. Collateral-driven credit cycles are a distinct mechanism, and that prize concerned banking and runs. I also think the committee should not penalise B027 for Acemoglu's 2024 recognition without a clear account of what is separately Autor's. A two-name Autor-Hanson award would hold up better on attribution than my own earlier three-name proposal, and I would take it seriously if B027 advances.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 (Mian and Sufi) first. He argues that the household-debt channel was not covered by the 2022 prize, that the evidence is replicated, and that the timing is ripe.
responses.response: I agree that the household-leverage channel is distinct from the bank-centred 2022 work, and the granular-data evidence has been influential. I still place B001 below the credit-cycles mechanism on maturity. The core papers are 2009-2017, and the dispute over credit supply versus expectations and demand channels is not settled. Their work is also arguably an empirical test and application of the collateral-and-leverage logic Kiyotaki and Moore laid out, so I see them as downstream of B006 and not as a substitute for it. I would revisit this in a few years.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B018 first and concedes that attribution among Calvo, Taylor, Woodford and others is contestable. He also flags that Gertler appears on both B018 and B006, which raises a double-counting question.
responses.response: I share the diagnosis that B018 is hard to credit cleanly, and that is the main reason I rank it below B006 despite its very large policy influence. On Gertler, I would not let his appearance on two ballots decide either one, because the two are distinct contributions. For B006 the originators' claim stands without him. If the committee wanted Gertler in B006, it should do so on the merits of his intermediation work, not because B018 is difficult to settle.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would read Kiyotaki-Moore as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
Whether Gertler, and possibly Gilchrist, should be added, and on what scientific basis.
How the committee weighs a mainly theoretical mechanism against the more directly empirical and policy-visible B027.
My own field proximity to finance and macro-finance may bias my weighting.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki or Moore is apparent from the supplied profile. I am an adjunct professor at Chicago Booth and have long overlap on this committee with Hassler and Krusell, who also hold views on this ballot; these are disclosed, not adjudicated. My Booth affiliation could create an institutional connection to candidates in other ballots (for example B001), none of which is in my preferred configuration. My principal co-author, Kaplan, is not credited on any shortlisted ballot.
